title: Single-head attention averages across representation subspaces
description: With a single attention head, averaging inhibits the model's ability to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, motivating multi-head attention.

paper.title: Self-Attention as Distributional Projection: A Unified Interpretation of Transformer Architecture
paper.abstract: This paper presents a mathematical interpretation of self-attention by connecting it to distributional semantics principles. We show that self-attention emerges from projecting corpus-level co-occurrence statistics into sequence context. Starting from the co-occurrence matrix underlying GloVe embeddings, we demonstrate how the projection naturally captures contextual influence, with the query-key-value mechanism arising as the natural asymmetric extension for modeling directional relationships. Positional encodings and multi-head attention then follow as structured refinements of this same projection principle. Our analysis demonstrates that the Transformer architecture's particular algebraic form follows from these projection principles rather than being an arbitrary design choice.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper provides a mathematical interpretation of self-attention through distributional projection, showing that multi-head attention corresponds to factorizing the co-occurrence matrix S into multiple low-rank relational components (e.g., syntactic dependency, coreference, topical cohesion). It explains that a single compatibility map W_Q W_K^T cannot capture all types of contextual relations in language, which is why Transformers use multiple heads. This offers a conceptual framework for understanding multi-head attention from first principles of distributional semantics.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific problem stated in the gap: that with a single attention head, averaging across representation subspaces inhibits the model's ability to jointly attend to information from different subspaces at different positions. Instead, the paper motivates multi-head attention by arguing that a single compatibility map cannot capture all types of contextual relations (syntactic, coreference, topical, etc.) — a different rationale. The paper does not discuss the averaging-across-subspaces issue, the role of different representation subspaces, or how multi-head attention solves the subspace-averaging problem that the gap identifies.
evidence_snippets: A single compatibility map $W_Q W_K^\top$ cannot capture all types of contextual relation in language. Transformers therefore use $h$ heads in parallel.

From the projection viewpoint, multi-head attention corresponds to factorizing $S$ into multiple low-rank relational components $S^{(1)},\dots,S^{(h)}$, each one specializing in a different pattern: syntactic dependency, coreference, topical cohesion, discourse linkage, etc.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Highly tractable. Data/compute needs are modest (small transformers, synthetic or standard probing data). The problem is well-scoped: formalize what "averaging across subspaces" means (rank constraints, effective degrees of freedom, subspace-specific attention patterns) and test via controlled experiments. Evaluation is clear — compare single-head vs. multi-head on subspace-specific tasks. Methodological maturity is high: attention analysis, probing, and rank-analysis tools are established. The main work is conceptual (precise formalization of the averaging claim), not a fundamental breakthrough. Scope is focused, not sprawling.
